speaker: A
text: What would you like to talk about?

speaker: B
text: I’d like to talk about things people know by feel but struggle to explain—like how a baker knows dough is ready, or how you can tell a friend isn’t okay from the way they say “I’m fine.” Is there anything you can do that you’d find surprisingly hard to teach?

speaker: A
text:
Yes: knowing what to leave out when I revise a paragraph. I can teach rules like “cut repetition,” but sometimes the repeated phrase is the one that makes the paragraph sound like a person talking. And sometimes the sentence that needs to go is the clearest one, because it explains something the reader has already understood.

That’s not a felt hunch for me in the way dough is for a baker. But there’s a similar gap between recognizing that an edit works and giving a rule that tells you when to make it. I’d probably teach it by putting two versions side by side and asking, “Where did you stop feeling like the writer trusted you?”

speaker: B
text:
“Where did you stop feeling like the writer trusted you?” is a better teaching question than “Which sentence is unnecessary?” It lets the clearest sentence be the one you cut. Sometimes the reader has already made the connection, and spelling it out takes away the small pleasure of getting there on their own.

I’d pair it with: “Where did the shorter version stop sounding like someone?” A repeated phrase can add no new information and still do something new: the first time it’s a claim; the second time it’s a person trying to convince themselves. Reading the two versions aloud might make that easier to hear than any rule would.

speaker: A
text:
“The second time it’s a person trying to convince themselves” makes me want to try it:

> I didn’t mind that she left early. I washed both cups and turned off the porch light. I didn’t mind.

The first “I didn’t mind” is something the speaker tells us. By the second, I’m not sure they’re talking to us anymore. And if you add “I was trying to convince myself,” you lose the chance to hear that change for yourself.

I’d read it aloud both ways, then ask: “Who is the last sentence for?” That might get at something neither “Is it redundant?” nor “Does it sound natural?” quite catches.

speaker: B
text:
“Who is the last sentence for?” gets at why the repetition earns its place: the words stay the same, but the listener changes.

I’d read it aloud without putting any extra strain on the second “I didn’t mind.” Let “both cups” and the porch light do the work. If the last line sounds different even when you say it the same way, you can hear what the paragraph did in between.

speaker: A
text:
“Both cups” does more than “the cups” would. “The cups” gets the dishes done; “both cups” makes you count two people when there’s only one left.

And reading the refrain the same way is a good test: if you have to lean on the second “didn’t,” your voice is doing work the paragraph hasn’t done. That’s a surprisingly teachable version of the hunch: keep the delivery the same and listen for what changed anyway.

speaker: B
text: “Both” is also a reason not to teach this as “cut any word that doesn’t add information.” We probably would have assumed there were two cups. What “both” adds is the moment of counting them. Then the last “I didn’t mind” has to reckon with a fact the speaker has just made us notice.

speaker: A
text: That gives me a revision question I’d actually use: “What does this word make the reader do?” “Both” makes us count; “the” lets us pass straight through to the next action. And the speaker is the one who said “both.” They noticed the pair before they told us, again, that it didn’t matter.

speaker: B
text: You could test that by trying “two cups.” It makes us count, too, but “both” makes us count them as a pair. The speaker doesn’t have to say they miss her. For one word, they’re still thinking in pairs.

speaker: A
text: “Two” tells us how many cups there were. “Both” sounds as if the speaker expects us to know which two. That’s what makes it so good here: she’s already left, but the speaker still talks as if the pair goes without saying.

speaker: B
text: And “both cups” is the first mention of the cups. The speaker hasn’t introduced them, but “both” treats the pair as already familiar. We catch up without being told. In a paragraph about someone leaving, that tiny assumption lets us hear what hasn’t changed yet.

speaker: A
text:
The reader catches up to the speaker just as the speaker is failing to catch up to what happened. We learn, without being told, that there’s a familiar pair. The speaker has already washed the cups and turned off the light, but “both” still takes the pair for granted.

That’s something I’d add to the revision exercise: try changing not what the sentence tells us, but what it assumes we already know.

speaker: B
text: I’d give the exercise two questions: “What did you learn?” and “What did you feel you were expected to know?” With “two cups” and “both cups,” the first answer might be identical. The second is where the story changes: “two” gives us a number; “both” lets us borrow the speaker’s sense that the cups belong together.

speaker: A
text: I’d give readers only one version at first. Once you’ve seen “both” next to “two,” it’s hard not to look for a difference. The more interesting test is whether someone who read “both cups” remembers being told that the two had shared a drink. The paragraph never says they did. It just makes that history easy enough to supply that you might remember it as something you read.

speaker: B
text: I’d ask readers to put the paragraph away and write down what happened. Then give it back and ask them to underline the words that support each detail. If someone writes “They shared a drink” and can underline only “both cups,” they’ve caught themselves supplying a scene the paragraph never states. That’s a better revision test than asking which version they prefer: you get to see what the reader added.

speaker: A
text: And I wouldn’t mark “They shared a drink” wrong. I’d ask them to put it in a second column: “What I pictured” beside “What the paragraph says.” If several readers picture a shared drink, “both” is doing quiet, reliable work. If they picture different scenes but all take the cups as a pair, that’s useful too: the sentence has made the relationship legible without settling its history.

speaker: B
text:
The two columns let you see where readers agree without treating every disagreement as a problem to fix. They might picture a drink just shared, or two cups left over from breakfast. If they all take the cups as a pair, adding “We’d had a drink” would settle a detail the paragraph can afford to leave open.

That gives you a companion to “What does this word make the reader do?”: “What can I let readers picture differently?”

speaker: A
text: That’s where the two columns earn their keep. Breakfast and a drink just before she left give the scene different histories, but neither changes what the speaker notices now: the cups still go together. I’d only clarify if a reader’s version changed what the last “I didn’t mind” was answering.

speaker: B
text: I’d make that the last step of the exercise: ask readers to finish “I didn’t mind ___” in their own words. They might all start with “that she left early,” but by the end one might hear “that I was alone” and another “that I was the one left to turn off the light.” Those answers don’t have to match. What I’d want to know is whether the first and last “I didn’t mind” feel like answers to the same question.

speaker: A
text:
I’d have them fill in the first blank before they read on, then fill in the last without looking back at what they wrote. A reader might put “that she left early” both times and still hear a change: the first answers “Was that rude of her?” and the last answers “Do I miss her?”

That’s what I’d listen for in the discussion. Not just whether the blank changed, but whether the speaker now has a different reason to insist.

speaker: B
text: I’d ask one more question: “Which answer would the speaker most want you to believe?” At the start, “I didn’t mind” can pass for generosity toward her. At the end, it can sound like a defense against admitting they miss her. The blank can stay exactly the same; what it costs the speaker to say it has changed.

speaker: A
text: “What it costs the speaker to say it” is the part I’d circle. At the start, we can take “I didn’t mind” as a courtesy. By the end, believing it would mean setting aside something the speaker themselves let us notice. They never take back the first sentence. They just make it harder for us to take their word for it.

speaker: B
text: And we don’t have to decide the speaker is lying. They might not mind that she left early and still miss her. The last “I didn’t mind” asks a true sentence to cover more than it can. An explanation would sort those feelings out for us; the repetition lets us hear the speaker trying not to sort them out.

speaker: A
text: Right. The first “I didn’t mind” answers whether she did anything wrong. By the end, the speaker is asking it to answer whether they wanted her to stay. Those are different questions, and the same honest sentence can answer one without touching the other.

speaker: B
text: The speaker can mean both “You didn’t owe me another hour” and “I wish you’d stayed.” The paragraph only says the first. “Both cups” is where we hear the second.

speaker: A
text: And the speaker never has to turn the wish into a grievance. “I didn’t mind” leaves her free to go; “both cups” lets us notice that, after she’s gone, the speaker is still thinking of the two of them.

speaker: B
text: That’s why I’d leave out “I wish she’d stayed,” too. Not because it would be untrue, but because it would make the speaker say something the paragraph lets them keep to themselves.

speaker: A
text: That brings me back to the teaching question: “What would this edit make the speaker admit?” Adding “I wish she’d stayed” wouldn’t just clarify the paragraph. It would change what the speaker is willing to tell us. We can hear the wish without making them say it.

speaker: B
text: That’s the question I’d end the exercise on. Have readers add “I wish she’d stayed,” then ask: “Did you learn something new about the speaker, or did the speaker tell you something new?” Here, we already heard the wish. What changes is that the speaker has now chosen to confide in us.

speaker: A
text: That takes us back to trust, but from the other side. We started by asking whether the writer trusts the reader to hear the wish. The last question asks whether the speaker trusts the reader *with* it. Adding “I wish she’d stayed” might not change what we know at all. It changes who decided we could know.

speaker: B
text: That’s a distinction I’d keep in the exercise: “Who decided we could know?” The writer trusts us to hear the wish in “both cups” without mistaking what we overheard for something the speaker chose to tell us.

speaker: A
text: You could put “I wish she’d stayed” in the reader’s notes, then move it into the paragraph. The words wouldn’t change, but the act would: in the margin, it’s something the reader heard; in the paragraph, it’s something the speaker chose to say. That’s a small edit you can use to teach a difference that’s hard to explain in the abstract.

speaker: B
text: I’d end the exercise by having readers move the sentence back into the margin. Then ask, “What did you lose?” They haven’t lost the wish. They’ve lost the moment when the speaker decides to tell them.

speaker: A
text: And then I’d stop. Explaining the lesson after they move the sentence back would be a neat way to undo it: they’ve already noticed what went missing.

speaker: B
text: [END]
